analysis.one_liner: Requires polluters to prove their permits won't harm nearby communities and lets residents sue over discriminatory pollution.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or vote; it died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have tightened civil rights law so that a program receiving federal money can be sued if it has a discriminatory effect, even without proof of intent, and would have given residents a direct right to sue. It would have required air and water pollution permits to account for the combined pollution already in a neighborhood, and to be denied unless there is a reasonable certainty of no harm to nearby residents. It also would have required ingredient labels on cosmetics and menstrual products, funded parks and transit-to-trails projects in underserved areas, and set up environmental justice offices, councils, and grant programs across the federal government.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities that bear disproportionate pollution. They would gain a private right of action under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, including for discriminatory effects rather than only intentional discrimination, plus attorney's fees and damages for intentional-discrimination claims. Permitting authorities would have to weigh cumulative exposure before issuing permits, and residents would get longer comment periods, community impact reports, and an EPA ombuds. The bill also funds urban park access, transit connections to public lands, and research on safer chemicals, and provides transition assistance to fossil-fuel-dependent communities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities of color and low-income areas near pollution

how_it_helps.text: Expands Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 to prohibit federally funded programs that cause disparate impacts based on race, color, or national origin, and lets aggrieved persons sue in federal district court without regard to amount in controversy.

Amends the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act so air and water permits may be denied unless there is a reasonable certainty of no harm to the general population or susceptible subpopulations, based on an analysis of cumulative impacts combined with existing pollution.
Requires permitting authorities to identify persistent violators, deny or condition their permits, and deny renewal to repeat violators whose compliance plans remain inadequate.

Requires community impact reports and at least 90-day public comment periods under the National Environmental Policy Act for federal actions that could affect environmental justice communities, and requires agencies to consider alternatives proposed by affected residents.
Requires ingredient lists or warnings on cosmetics and menstrual products and funds research on safer alternatives to toxic chemicals in consumer, cleaning, toy, and baby products.

Creates grant programs for park access and transit-to-trails connections in underserved communities, an EPA environmental justice ombuds, a White House environmental justice interagency council, and agency environmental justice strategies.

analysis.who_pays: Industrial facilities seeking air and water permits would bear new analysis requirements and face permit denials based on cumulative impacts, with the burden on the applicant to demonstrate no harm. Cosmetics and menstrual product makers would face new labeling obligations. Federal agencies would bear new reporting, strategy, and community-engagement requirements, and taxpayers would fund the new grant programs, including $10 million per year authorized for transit-to-trails.
analysis.who_pays_short: Polluting industries, cosmetics makers, and federal agencies

drawbacks.text: The permit standard denies air and water permits unless the applicant can show a reasonable certainty of no harm after accounting for cumulative impacts — a demanding test that could make many permits difficult or impossible to obtain, including for projects such as energy or manufacturing facilities a community may want or need.
The bill creates new private rights of action and judicial review, which would invite extensive litigation over federal actions and permits and could delay projects through court challenges.

Park and transit-to-trails grants generally require a matching contribution equal to 100 percent of the federal amount, although the Secretary may waive the match, which could strain small towns' budgets.

Agencies would face substantial new duties — strategies, annual reports, ombuds staff, community impact reports, and mapping tools — whose costs and administrative burden the bill does not fully quantify.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents of pollution-burdened communities the benefits are substantial: enforceable legal rights, permits that weigh the pollution they already live with, and access to parks and safer products. The costs fall mostly on permit applicants and manufacturers, and the strict no-harm standard and expanded litigation rights carry a real risk of slowing infrastructure — including clean energy projects — that some communities would accept. The trade-off is real but the bill's core aim, letting people who breathe the air and drink the water affect permitting decisions, addresses a burden that current law largely leaves on the communities themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Duckworth introduced the bill on March 22, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; the congressional record shows no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote.
The bill had 14 cosponsors, all Democrats or Independents: 13 of the Senate's 48 Democrats and 1 of its 4 Independents, with no Republican support.

The bill would have let individuals sue over discriminatory effects of federally funded programs and would have allowed permits to be denied unless applicants showed a reasonable certainty of no harm from cumulative pollution exposure.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies seeking air and water pollution permits are better off, because the stricter cumulative-impact permitting standard, persistent-violator provisions, and Title VI disparate-impact liability never took effect. Communities near pollution sources remain under the pre-existing rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Industrial permit applicants avoiding stricter reviews

for.name: Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it stalled in committee.

against.what_they_did: No Senate Republican cosponsored the bill, and none acted to advance it.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents and no Republican signed on; with Democrats holding 48 of 100 Senate seats, the bill lacked the coalition needed to reach the floor.

industries.note: The bill would have let regulators deny or condition air and water permits based on cumulative neighborhood pollution and would have imposed plans and permit denials on repeat violators, shifting the burden of proving safety to the applicant. Its failure leaves existing permit practices in place.

industries.industry: Cosmetics and personal care product makers
industries.note: The bill would have required ingredient labeling and warnings on cosmetics and menstrual products and funded research into safer alternatives. Consumers would have gained ingredient transparency the industry currently is not required to provide.

industries.industry: Major infrastructure and energy project developers
industries.note: Community impact reports, 90-day comment periods, and cumulative-impact permitting would have added analysis requirements and litigation risk to federal approvals, slowing projects including potentially clean energy ones. The bill also would have subsidized transition assistance for fossil-fuel-dependent communities.

industries.industry: Environmental justice and community advocacy organizations
industries.note: The bill would have given these groups standing to sue, seats on advisory councils, technical assistance funding, and a formal role in federal permitting and agency strategy processes. Its death leaves their legal toolkit unchanged.
